Plant the Moon Challenge Final Report 
Team Name: Astrogrow Team ID #: 19032 
Coach Name: Jiang Li Challenge Division: High School 
 
Introduction 
NASA (the National Aeronautics and Space Administration) is developing the Artemis 
program with the goal of establishing the first long-term lunar base settlement on the 
Moon, which will become a stepping stone for Mars development. Artemis astronauts will 
carry plants to the moon to study plant growth on a lunar surface, using resources found on 
the Moon to develop food sources. 
The Plant the Moon challenge is a competition to grow edible plants on lunar regolith (the 
moon's top layer of dust and gravel), measuring the capability of lunar regolith for growing 
crops. The knowledge gathered can contribute to establishing a base on the moon for 
further space research and exploration. 
Prior experiments show that growth is challenging on lunar soil. It does not contain the 
carbon and nitrogen that plants need and its phosphorus is mostly inaccessible [1], 
although scientists at the University of Florida have successfully grown the 
plant Arabidopsis in lunar soil collected on the Apollo 11, 12 and 17 missions [2]. However, 
it isn’t an edible plant, and it is also proved that most crops cannot grow in 100% lunar 
regolith. To grow edible crops in lunar regolith, various experiments done in previous Plant 
the Moon Challenge seasons show that the most common ways are to add various 
additives to the lunar soil. 
The Southern CASE Research Team used 50%-85% peat moss as an additive [3]. 
The Ozarks Team used a mixture of 50% regolith and 50% mycorrhizal fungi [4]. 
The West Bluejays - D team used 50% lunar regolith and 50% of a topsoil mixture with 
varying urea fertilizer levels [5]. 
The KCA Moon Planters team’s research shows if regolith is mixed with 33.3% seed starter 
(organic compost) with the proper water amount, mung bean sprouts will grow well [6]. 
The Sunburst Big Brains team used different additives (organic compost, liquid fertilizer, 
potting soil at varying percentages) which showed that 30%-40% organic compost mixed 
with lunar regolith produces encouraging results [7].

The Minnesota West Bluejays team successfully used 25% topsoil and 75% lunar regolith 
with various types of solid nitrogen sources [8]. 
While additives seem to be necessary, we plan to utilize less additives with the goal of 
growing crops in largely extraterrestrial soil. We plan to use 33% compost mixed with moon 
regolith (a 1:2 ratio) for our experiment. 
 
Purpose 
The purpose of this experiment is to determine if companion planting can improve lunar 
soil and utilize lunar space at the same efficiency as Earth soil. 
Benefit of companion planting: 
In farm practices, people found growing several types of crops near one another can 
enhance crop production. Utilizing companion planting is not only beneficial for your 
plants, but also helps maximize your space. 
 
Experimental Parameters 
Variables: Because there is so much variation, each group will have two pots so we can 
take the average for better comparison 
Independent variables: 
Light and water amount, temperature, lunar regolith mixture with potatoes and soybeans 
Dependent variables: 
Plant growth: plant’s growth rate and height, number of leaves, and life length 
Control Variables: 
100% compost soil with potatoes and soybeans 
 
Project Hypothesis 
We expect that the pots with potato planted with a companion crop (soybeans) will have 
better or equal growth to pots with the two crops planted separately, as measured by plant

height over the growth period. Even if they have the same growth for both, planting them 
together utilizes the space better than planting the two different crops separately. 
 
Experimental Design & Procedures 
Because of weather variations in California over the duration of the experiment, the 
outdoor temperature will be cold, especially at night, which will affect the plants’ abilities 
to grow. The experiment will thus be set up indoors and inside a temperature chamber with 
growing lights to keep them warm at nighttime. This will help to determine if potatoes grown 
with companion crops will have an advantage in lunar regolith. 
1. Set up a growth temperature chamber to keep a constant temperature over fall and 
winter, using grow lights for 24 hours to simulate a lunar greenhouse which can use 
solar power to maintain light all day for growth acceleration.

2. Use 100% compost soil for the control groups. For the groups containing the lunar 
regolith, create a soil mixture with a 1:2 ratio of compost soil to lunar regolith. 
3. Soak the seeds in a bowl of water for 24 hours (without sunlight). 
4. Plant the seeds in the pots. 
5. Check and document pH, temperature, and moisture 2 times a week. 
 4-in-1 meter to measure the parameters to make sure the environment is optimal for 
plant growth 
 
 
 
 
6. Document plant height and leaf number each week. 
7. Analyze data at the end of the experiment. 
 
Groups: 
In total, 2 pots as the controls and 2 for comparison 
1. Control groups (100% compost soil) 
Potato seeds planted with soybean seeds (2 pots) 
 
2. Test groups (33% compost and 66% lunar regolith)

Growing report and challenge

From week 1-3, the main challenges we experienced were: 
• Most of the potted seeds we brought from Amazon didn’t germinate or died soon 
after germination 
• We dug out the seeds that didn’t germinate and found that most of them were rotten 
 
Rotten soybean seed 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
• Two of the soybean seeds germinated in week 2 but died after one week. After 
digging them out, we found that they developed 7-centimeter roots but no leaves, 
meaning that they died after all the nutrition was consumed by the seed.

• One soybean seed growing in the mixed lunar regolith (POT 3) germinated and grew 
well, reaching abut 25cm by Week 5, but none of the soybeans in the Earth soil have 
grown, implying that the root cause of the seeds failing to thrive is not the mixed 
lunar soil but the seed quality 
 
 
 
• To combat this, we bought another batch of seeds from Home Depot to start again 
in Week 3 to improve seed germination. Though the standard procedure is to bury 
the seeds at a depth of 1-2 cm, the lunar regolith has a very high density after 
watering which makes it difficult for the seeds to break past the surface during 
growth. Instead, we buried the seeds at a shallower depth of 0.5 cm and covered 
them with mulch to help maintain moisture. Also, we noticed that the lunar regolith 
does not retain much water or air which are vital to seed growth. To fix this issue, we 
used a 3D-printer to print tubes with holes and inserted them in the lunar regolith 
soil to improve retention.

Tube SolidWorks 3D Model and Cross Section 
 
Final Printed Tube (Using the Bambu A1 Combo Model 3D-printer) 
 
 
• Following these improvements, we observed that some pots of soybeans and 
potatoes successfully began to germinate and grow.

Conclusion 
 
1) Companion planting is a valid method to grow two different plants in a limited 
space, allowing more efficient use of space. However, stronger growing lights are 
needed to provide adequate light for both plants and better water management. 
2) Using tubes with holes can help distribution of water and air through the lunar 
regolith to reduce seed death and improve plant growth. 
3) When comparing plant height and leaf numbers, 100% earth soil has much better 
growth than the lunar regolith mixture. 
4) We noticed that seeds planted in lunar regolith have much higher rotten seed rates 
(2 out 4) vs. 100% earth soil (1 out 4). 
5) To plant in lunar regolith, the seeds should be buried at a shallower depth than in 
earth soil to improve seed germination. 
 
Future Discussions 
 
1) More research and experimentation should be conducted to find the best addition 
to lunar regolith to improve water and air retention. The next step we suggest is to try 
toilet paper or even small foam balls as additives 
2) Our experiment was limited by a small growth population and thus cannot be 
confidently generalized to all experiments. Further research with more control and 
experiment groups are needed to develop a better understanding. 
3) Future experimentation with various types of plants for companion planting will 
allow for a more in-depth comprehension of the ideal combination for plant growth 
in lunar regolith.
